newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: World's islands fear global warming will drown them.
newsitem.headline: World's islands fear global warming will drown them.

text.p: Small island nations issued a cry for help at a U.N. Earth Summit on Tuesday, saying they were rapidly becoming the first victims of global warming and could disappear under the sea.
"This affects us first and it affects us in the most profound and dangerous way," said Tuiloma Neroni Slade, Western Samoa's U.N. ambassador and head of the Alliance of Small Island States..

"The people know things are changing. They are experiencing a very unusually high rainfall, very hot air temperatures. From my part of the world, the frequency of these events is something quite unusual," he told a news conference.

The small island nations, including the Indian Ocean Maldives, Cyprus, Caribbean states and Pacific archipelagos, say their survival is threatened by the rise of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases, produced mainly by developed industrial states.
Scientists predict sea levels will rise between 12 inches (30 centimetres) and 40 inches (100 centimetres) over the next century as the planet grows warmer, if greenhouse gases are not reduced.
The rise of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases in the atmosphere contributes to the melting of polar ice caps, which raises the level of the oceans.
Several island representatives said the damage was already well under way.
The five-day 173-nation conference, including more than 60 prime ministers and presidents, is taking stock of progress since the first Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro in 1992.

Micronesia's President Jacob Nena said some smaller atolls had already been abandoned. His country's main island, Nukuoro, was inundated with salt water that ruined taro patches, a vital source of local food.
"Help us, help all of us, including yourselves," he said.
Rich countries, responsible for more than half the world's pollution, have not been able to agree on new targets for reducing greenhouse gases before a December climate conference in Kyoto, Japan.
President Maumoon Abdul Gayoom of the Maldives said he had been talking about the issue for 10 years but "the threat to my country has remained as alarming and as urgent as ever."
Slade said: "The people know that the homes and infrastructures are being damaged. They know they are unable to get insurance because the insurance companies are not there."

The Europeans have set specific goals but neither the United States, Canada nor Japan have agreed to their target of reducing emissions by 15 percent below 1990 levels by 2,010. The small island states want this raised to 20 percent.
President Bill Clinton will address the body on Thursday and speak about the long-term need to stabilise greenhouse gases, U.S. officials said. But he would give no short-term targets.
Commenting on the lack of commitments, Slade said:
"We submit, with all respect, that they must. They must. Otherwise they put our lives and communities at risk."

Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien told the conference his country would "not meet the year 2,000 targets for stabilising greenhouse gas emissions" because the structure "of our economy poses particular challenges in this regard."
He told reporters later that the goals set at Rio five years ago to reduce emissions to 1990 levels had not been met by other rich states either.

Only Germany, he said, could reduce its pollution because it had closed coal-burning and other facilities in the former East Germany. Britain, he said, had discovered natural gas and decreased its dependency on other fossil fuels.

Cuba's parliamentary speaker, Ricardo Alarcon, a former foreign minister said "capitalist greed" was the main cause "of the severe damage to nature which is threatening the survival of humankind today."
